concepts.name: Problem contract extraction
concepts.description: Extract output semantics, structural constraints, scale, mutation rules, and memory limits before choosing an algorithm.

concepts.name: Traceable brute-force baseline
concepts.description: Start from the simplest clearly correct solution so repeated work is visible.

concepts.name: Baseline → bottleneck → maintained state
concepts.description: Start from a correct baseline, identify repeated expensive work, then maintain the information that removes it.

concepts.name: Growth-rate reasoning
concepts.description: Use asymptotic growth as a scale filter.

concepts.name: Aggregate operation counting
concepts.description: Count total pointer moves/operations across the full run rather than relying on loop nesting.

concepts.name: Repeated-work elimination
concepts.description: Cache, index, maintain, or incrementally update information the baseline repeatedly recomputes.

concepts.name: Invariant and progress rule
concepts.description: State what remains true and what strictly moves toward termination.

concepts.name: Counterexample-driven edge testing
concepts.description: Use tiny hostile cases to attack assumptions and boundaries.

questions.prompt: A batch deduper currently checks whether any event ID repeats. Before choosing a faster design, which missing facts could materially change the implementation?
questions.explanation: Scale, mutation rules, and memory constraints can change which optimizations are legal or worthwhile. Local variable naming does not change the algorithmic contract.
hints: Ask whether the answer or implementation would change if this detail changed.

error_codes.description: At least one relevant clarification was missed.
At least one irrelevant clarification was selected.

questions.prompt: You inherited a duplicate detector and want a tiny, obviously correct reference implementation for differential testing before optimizing it. Which approach is the best reference baseline?
questions.explanation: A pairwise comparison is simple and correct, so it gives you a concrete O(n²) baseline. You can then identify repeated membership/search work and optimize deliberately.
hints: Choose the explanation that is obviously correct before worrying about the final optimization.

error_codes.description: The selected opening skips or weakens the correct-baseline reasoning.

choice_feedback.pairwise: Correct: a simple independent oracle is valuable precisely because it is easy to reason about.
choice_feedback.sort_now: Sorting may be a valid final approach, but mutating/reordering before checking the contract is a poor reference baseline.
choice_feedback.binary_search: Binary search does not apply directly to an unsorted array.
choice_feedback.hash_magic: A reference implementation should ideally fail differently from the optimized implementation, not share its core state logic.

choices.label: Compare every distinct pair. It is O(n²), but its behavior is easy to verify.
Sort the production input in place and compare neighbors, without first checking whether mutation/order is allowed.
For each value, binary-search the still-unsorted original array.
Use the same hash-set optimization you are trying to verify, so both implementations share the same state/update risks.

questions.prompt:
A reviewer made four claims about this two-pointer loop. Flag the incorrect claim.

```python
left = 0
for right in range(n):
    while left < right and invalid(left, right):
        left += 1
```

Assume `invalid(...)` is O(1).
questions.explanation: The inner loop is amortized across the full run because `left` never moves backward.
hints: Count total pointer moves, not syntactic nesting.

error_codes.description: The selected line is not the one that breaks the algorithm.

questions.prompt: Which TWO code patterns can create O(n²) work when performed for each of n input items?
questions.explanation: A full list membership scan and `list.index` are both linear in the list length; placing either inside another n-scale loop can produce quadratic work. Constant arithmetic and one pre-loop sort do not have that shape.
hints: Look for an O(n)-scale operation repeated O(n) times.

error_codes.description: One repeated linear operation was missed.
A non-quadratic shape was selected.

questions.prompt:
Assume `should_drop(...)` is O(1). Why can this still be O(n) total work even though a `while` loop is nested inside a `for` loop?

```python
left = 0
for right in range(len(values)):
    while left < right and should_drop(left, right):
        left += 1
```
questions.explanation: Count pointer movement across the entire run. Neither pointer moves backward, so the total number of pointer advances is O(n).
hints: How many times can `left` increase during the entire function?

error_codes.description: The selected answer does not match the algorithm's actual behavior.

source_refs.title: MIT OpenCourseWare 6.006 — Lecture 1: Algorithms and Computation

choice_feedback.aggregate: Correct. Aggregate pointer movement is linear.
choice_feedback.nested: Loop nesting alone does not determine complexity when the inner loop shares monotonic state.
choice_feedback.once: A single right step may cause several left moves.
choice_feedback.constant: Each increment is O(1), but there can be O(n) increments.

choices.label: `right` moves forward n times and `left` also moves forward at most n times total
Any nested loop is automatically O(n²)
The `while` loop can execute only once for each `right`
Because `left += 1` makes the whole algorithm O(1)

questions.prompt: The input is sorted. The search uses an inclusive interval `[left, right]`. Flag the update that can fail to make progress when `mid == left`.
questions.explanation: `left = mid` can leave left unchanged, so the candidate interval may never shrink. When `values[mid] < target`, mid is known not to be the target, so `left = mid + 1` both preserves the candidate invariant and makes progress.
hints: Try a two-element interval where mid evaluates to left.

error_codes.description: The non-progressing boundary update was not identified.
A valid search step was incorrectly flagged.

source_refs.title: Cornell CS 2112 — Loop invariants

questions.prompt: In an inclusive binary-search interval, `values[mid] < target`. Why is `left = mid + 1` the useful update?
questions.explanation: Sorted order proves that indices through mid cannot contain the target. Moving to mid + 1 discards only impossible candidates and strictly shrinks the interval.
hints: The update must satisfy two jobs: preserve possible answers and make the interval smaller.

error_codes.description: The selected reason does not capture both invariant preservation and progress.

source_refs.title: Cornell CS 2112 — Loop invariants

choice_feedback.both: Correct: the update is justified by sorted order and also guarantees progress.
choice_feedback.style: This is a correctness/progress requirement, not a style preference.
choice_feedback.skip: The midpoint is not skipped arbitrarily; it has been proven too small.
choice_feedback.runtime: It does not make the loop constant time.

choices.label: It removes only candidates proven too small and guarantees the interval shrinks
It is only the conventional coding style for binary search
It skips an arbitrary midpoint to make the code faster
It makes the remaining loop O(1)

questions.prompt: A sorted version index contains `[2, 5, 8, 12, 19]`. A lookup for version key 12 uses inclusive binary search. Order the states the search visits.
questions.explanation: The first midpoint is index 2 with value 8, so the target must be to the right. The interval becomes [3,4]; midpoint 3 is value 12, so the search succeeds.
hints: Compute the midpoint of [0,4], apply the comparison, then compute the midpoint of the remaining interval.

error_codes.description: The candidate interval trace is out of order.
